jhmt-2019-probcombo-01.title: Fix one man, permute the rest
jhmt-2019-probcombo-01.body: Men and women must alternate. Fix one man to remove rotational equivalence: $(4-1)! = 6$ ways to seat the remaining 3 men in the remaining men's seats. The 4 women fill the 4 gaps between the men in $4! = 24$ ways. Total: $6 \times 24 = \boxed{144}$.

jhmt-2019-probcombo-02.title: Bayes' theorem
jhmt-2019-probcombo-02.body:
By Bayes' theorem:
$$P(\text{die}=3 \mid 2 \text{ heads}) = \frac{P(\text{die}=3)\cdot P(2\text{ heads} \mid 3\text{ flips})}{P(2\text{ heads})}$$

$P(\text{die}=3)\cdot P(2\text{ heads}\mid 3) = \tfrac{1}{6}\cdot\tfrac{\binom{3}{2}}{2^3} = \tfrac{1}{6}\cdot\tfrac{3}{8} = \tfrac{1}{16}$.

$P(2\text{ heads}) = \tfrac{1}{6}\sum_{n=2}^{6}\frac{\binom{n}{2}}{2^n} = \tfrac{1}{6}\cdot\frac{16+24+24+20+15}{64} = \tfrac{1}{6}\cdot\tfrac{99}{64} = \tfrac{33}{128}$.

$P(\text{die}=3\mid 2\text{ heads}) = \dfrac{1/16}{33/128} = \dfrac{8}{33}$.

So $p+q = 8+33 = \boxed{41}$.

jhmt-2019-probcombo-03.title: Identify D(2019) then count
jhmt-2019-probcombo-03.body:
$2019 = 3 \times 673$ where 673 is prime, so $D(2019) = 673$.

For any $n$, $D(n) = n/p_\min(n)$ where $p_\min$ is the smallest prime factor. $D(n) > 673$ requires $n/p_\min > 673$.

- If $p_\min = 2$: $n/2 > 673 \Leftrightarrow n > 1346 \Leftrightarrow n \ge 1348$ (even). Even $n$ from 1348 to 2018: $\frac{2018-1348}{2}+1 = 336$ values.
- If $p_\min = 3$: $n > 2019$, impossible for $n \le 2019$.
- For larger primes: similarly impossible.

So $P = 336/2019 = 112/673$ (dividing by $\gcd = 3$). $m + n = 112 + 673 = \boxed{785}$.

jhmt-2019-probcombo-04.title: Gambler's ruin
jhmt-2019-probcombo-04.body: Let $p_x$ be the probability of reaching $-3$ before $5$ starting from $x$. Then $p_{-3}=1$, $p_5=0$, and $p_x=\frac12(p_{x-1}+p_{x+1})$ for $-3<x<5$, so $p_x$ is linear in $x$: $p_x=\frac{5-x}{8}$. Hence $p_0=\frac58$ and $m+n=5+8=\boxed{13}$.

jhmt-2019-probcombo-05.title: Linearity of expectation
jhmt-2019-probcombo-05.body:
By linearity of expectation, $E = 7 \cdot P(\text{at least one student chooses a given day}) = 7\left(1 - \left(\tfrac{6}{7}\right)^5\right)$.

$= 7 - \tfrac{6^5}{7^4} = \tfrac{7^5 - 6^5}{7^4} = \tfrac{16807 - 7776}{2401} = \tfrac{9031}{2401}$.

Since $2401 = 7^4$ and $9031 \equiv 1 \pmod{7}$ (as $7 \times 1290 = 9030$), $\gcd(9031, 2401) = 1$.

$m + n = 9031 + 2401 = \boxed{11432}$.

jhmt-2019-probcombo-06.title: Biased random walk
jhmt-2019-probcombo-06.body:
Write $a_i=100\cdot2^{e_i}$, where $e_0=0$ and each step changes $e$ by $-1$ (probability $\frac14$) or $+1$ (probability $\frac34$). Since $100\cdot2^{-6}=\frac{100}{64}\ge1$ and $100\cdot2^{-7}=\frac{100}{128}<1$, the sequence is finite exactly when $e$ ever reaches $-7$.

Let $r$ be the probability that the walk ever goes one level below its current level. Conditioning on the first step, $r=\frac14+\frac34r^2$, whose roots are $r=1$ and $r=\frac13$; since the walk drifts upward, $r<1$, so $r=\frac13$. (Formally, $r$ is the smallest nonnegative root, as it is the limit of the probabilities of dropping within $N$ steps, which are all at most $\frac13$ by induction.) Dropping $7$ levels requires $7$ independent such drops, so the probability is $\left(\frac13\right)^7=\frac1{2187}$, and $m+n=\boxed{2188}$.

jhmt-2019-probcombo-07.title: Markov chain on cube
jhmt-2019-probcombo-07.body:
By symmetry, classify vertices by distance from the start: State 0 (start), State 1 (3 adjacent vertices), State 2 (3 vertices adjacent to the opposite), State 3 (target, opposite vertex).

Transitions:
- From State 0: always moves to State 1.
- From State 1 (e.g., vertex 001 in binary): neighbors are State 0 (vertex 000) with prob $1/3$, and two State 2 vertices with prob $2/3$.
- From State 2 (e.g., vertex 011): neighbors are two State 1 vertices (prob $2/3$) and State 3 (target, prob $1/3$).

Let $E_i$ = expected moves to reach State 3 from State $i$.
$$E_2 = 1 + \tfrac{2}{3}E_1$$
$$E_1 = 1 + \tfrac{1}{3}E_0 + \tfrac{2}{3}E_2 = 1 + \tfrac{1}{3}(1+E_1) + \tfrac{2}{3}\left(1+\tfrac{2}{3}E_1\right) = 2 + \tfrac{7}{9}E_1$$
$$\Rightarrow E_1 = 9,\quad E_2 = 7,\quad E_0 = 1 + E_1 = 10.$$
The expected number of moves is $\boxed{10}$.

jhmt-2019-probcombo-08.title: Recurrence on parity
jhmt-2019-probcombo-08.body:
Let $f(n)$ be the probability that the sum is odd when the current (and first) term is $n$, so $f(1)=1$. From $n>1$ the next term $m$ is uniform on $\{1,\dots,n-1\}$ and the total is $n$ plus the total of the process started at $m$. With $S(k)=f(1)+\dots+f(k)$:
$$f(n)=\frac{S(n-1)}{n-1}\ (n\text{ even}),\qquad f(n)=1-\frac{S(n-1)}{n-1}\ (n\text{ odd}).$$
**Claim:** $S(2k-1)=k$ for all $k\ge1$. True for $k=1$. If $S(2k-1)=k$, then $f(2k)=\frac{k}{2k-1}$, $S(2k)=\frac{2k^2}{2k-1}$, $f(2k+1)=1-\frac{k}{2k-1}=\frac{k-1}{2k-1}$, and
$$S(2k+1)=\frac{2k^2+k-1}{2k-1}=\frac{(2k-1)(k+1)}{2k-1}=k+1.$$
So $f(2k+1)=\frac{k-1}{2k-1}$; for $2019=2\cdot1009+1$ this gives $f(2019)=\frac{1008}{2017}$. Since $2017$ is prime the fraction is in lowest terms, and $p+q=\boxed{3025}$.

jhmt-2019-probcombo-09.title: Burnside's lemma
jhmt-2019-probcombo-09.body:
The rotation group of a cube has 24 elements. Count colorings fixed by each type:

| Rotation type | Count | Fixed colorings |
|---|---|---|
| Identity | 1 | $3^6 = 729$ |
| 90°/270° around face axis | 6 | $3^3 = 27$ |
| 180° around face axis | 3 | $3^4 = 81$ |
| 120°/240° around vertex axis | 8 | $3^2 = 9$ |
| 180° around edge-midpoint axis | 6 | $3^3 = 27$ |

By Burnside: $\frac{1}{24}(729 + 6\cdot 27 + 3\cdot 81 + 8\cdot 9 + 6\cdot 27) = \frac{1368}{24} = \boxed{57}$.

jhmt-2019-probcombo-10.title: Count cycles by size in K_{7,7}
jhmt-2019-probcombo-10.body:
Every left vertex is joined to every right vertex, so the picture is the complete bipartite graph $K_{7,7}$. A cycle alternates sides, so it uses some $k\ge2$ vertices from each side. Given the chosen $2k$ vertices, list the cycle starting at a fixed left vertex: the other $k-1$ left vertices can appear in $(k-1)!$ orders and the $k$ right vertices in $k!$ orders, and each cycle is listed twice (once per direction). So there are $\frac{(k-1)!\,k!}{2}$ cycles on those vertices, and in total
$$\sum_{k=2}^{7}\binom7k^2\frac{(k-1)!\,k!}{2}=441+7350+88200+635040+2116800+1814400=\boxed{4662231}.$$
(For $k=2,\dots,7$: $\binom7k^2=441,1225,1225,441,49,1$ and $\frac{(k-1)!k!}{2}=1,6,72,1440,43200,1814400$.)
